items.definition: The title of a newspaper or online article, printed in large letters at the top.
examples: The headline said the minister had resigned, but the story was more complicated.
I only had time to read the headlines on my phone this morning.

items.definition: A newspaper with small pages, short articles and lots of photos, which often focuses on celebrities and scandal.
examples: The tabloids ran the story on their front pages for a week.
He never reads the tabloids, because he finds them too sensational.

items.definition: To send out a programme on television or radio, or online, so that people can watch or listen to it.
examples: The match will be broadcast live on radio and television.
The speech was broadcast to millions of viewers around the world.

items.definition: The amount and kind of attention that newspapers, television and other news sources give to an event or a subject.
examples: The election received wide coverage in the national press.
Many viewers complained about the one-sided coverage of the strike.

items.definition: Newspapers and magazines, and the journalists who write for them.
examples: Freedom of the press is essential in a democracy.
The actress refused to speak to the press after the trial.

items.definition: To pay regularly in order to receive a newspaper, magazine, channel or online service.
examples: I subscribe to a weekly magazine about science.
Many people have cancelled the channels they subscribed to because of rising prices.

items.definition: The official control of what people can see, read or say, by removing material considered offensive or dangerous.
examples: The film was banned in several countries because of government censorship.
Online platforms are often accused of censorship when they delete posts.

items.definition: Showing support for one side in an unfair way, so that the information is not balanced.
examples: Critics say the channel is biased against the government.
A biased report only gives you half of the story.

items.definition: To spread very quickly and widely on the internet because lots of people share it.
examples: Her short video went viral and was seen by millions overnight.
Nobody expected the joke to go viral.

items.definition: False stories that look like real news and are spread online to mislead people.
examples: Schools should teach students how to spot fake news.
A lot of fake news spreads because people share articles without reading them.

items.definition: An online headline or picture designed to make you click on a link, although the content is often disappointing.
examples: I fell for the clickbait again, and the article said nothing new.
The site is full of clickbait headlines about celebrities.

items.definition: A person, document or organisation that provides information, especially for a news story.
examples: The journalist refused to name her source.
Always check where the information comes from before you trust a source.
collocations: a source close to the minister

items.definition: To watch or listen to a particular television or radio programme.
examples: Millions of people tuned in to watch the final.
Tune in tomorrow at nine for the full interview.

items.definition: Describing news or reports that exaggerate in order to shock people and attract attention.
examples: The programme was criticised for its sensationalist coverage of the accident.
He accused the paper of sensationalist reporting.

items.definition: An article in a newspaper that gives the opinion of the editor or the newspaper on a current issue.
examples: The editorial argued that the government should cut fuel taxes.
I always read the editorial before the other articles.

trap.en: A company that publishes books is a publisher or a publishing house, not an editorial. In English an editorial is a newspaper opinion article.
trap.es: La empresa que publica libros es a publisher o a publishing house. Editorial, en inglés, es el artículo de opinión de un periódico.
